title: Curiosity and Science Learning
author: Dynamic Learning
summary: The author surveys recent research on the psychology of curiosity to ask how much it actually drives learning and long-term knowledge growth, distinguishing curiosity that helps memory encoding from curiosity that constitutes genuine learning. Drawing on Jordan Litman's distinction between I-type curiosity (enjoyment-driven, sustained exploration) and D-type curiosity (deprivation-driven, targeted question-asking), the piece centers on a 2025 longitudinal study by Koeber and Osterhaus that followed 122 children from the start of primary school through Grades 3-4 to see whether either type predicted later scientific reasoning and knowledge, beyond prior competence and intelligence. The study found both types predicted early scientific reasoning, but this relationship weakened by Grade 4, while I-type curiosity showed a more durable relationship with accumulated science knowledge across the primary years -- suggesting a developmental 'reweighting' where D-type curiosity resolves immediate uncertainty and I-type curiosity sustains long-term engagement. The author closes by speculatively connecting this to the SEEK (Schema Expansion and Error-driven Knowledge-building) model, proposing that D-type curiosity is especially sensitive to prediction error while I-type curiosity supports steady, lower-friction schema tuning.
points: The piece distinguishes I-type curiosity (enjoyment-driven, sustained exploration) from D-type curiosity (deprivation-driven, targeted question-asking), following psychologist Jordan Litman's framework.

A 2025 longitudinal study of 122 children (Koeber & Osterhaus) found both curiosity types predicted early scientific reasoning, but the relationship weakened by Grade 4 while I-type curiosity remained more consistently linked to accumulated science knowledge.
The author notes curiosity's predictive effects held even after accounting for prior knowledge and non-verbal intelligence, though the effect sizes were small.

The piece proposes a tentative link to the SEEK model, speculating D-type curiosity is especially sensitive to prediction error while I-type curiosity supports steadier, lower-friction schema tuning over time.
quotes: Several studies have found that state curiosity (temporary, extrinsic and goal directed, rather than internal and stable trait curiosity) can enhance memory encoding and later retention (e.g. Gruber, 2014; Fandakova & Gruber, 2021). So there seems to be ample evidence that curiosity helps us remember stuff. Remembering doesn't on its own, however, constitute learning.

Litman calls these I-type curiosity and D-type curiosity. I-type curiosity is associated with broad enjoyment, positive affect and sustained exploration in content-rich materials, resulting in the gradual accumulation of conceptual knowledge.

Results indicated that curiosity isn't a single, uniform influence. Early scientific reasoning was found to be associated with both I-type and D-type curiosity, especially in the early school years. But the relationship weakened by Grade 4.

The authors suggest a developmental reweighting. D-type curiosity may be especially useful for resolving immediate uncertainty and supporting inquiry, while I-type curiosity might be more important for sustained engagement and long-term knowledge growth.
We might speculate that D-type curiosity is particularly sensitive to prediction error. I-type curiosity doesn't necessarily require such a strongly aversive knowledge gap.
